Question 113 (Barium Nitrate, Ba(NO₃)₂)
Part A
(i) Ground-state electron configuration of Ba²⁺
Barium (Ba, atomic number 56) loses 2 valence electrons to form Ba²⁺.Answer: [Xe] (or full configuration: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶4d¹⁰5s²5p⁶)
(ii) Why is the radius of Ba²⁺ smaller than Ba atom?
A neutral Ba atom has 6 electron shells; Ba²⁺ loses its outermost 2 electrons, leaving 5 electron shells.
The nuclear charge is unchanged, but fewer electron shells reduce electron shielding. The remaining electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus, so the ionic radius shrinks.
Part B
Additional measurement: Initial temperature of water and final temperature of the solution after dissolution.Laboratory equipment: Thermometer
Part C
Calculate ΔHₛₒₗᵤₜᵢₒₙ (kJ/mol)Given: Heat transferred (q) = 8480 J = 8.48 kJ (endothermic, so q > 0)ΔHₛₒₗᵤₜᵢₒₙ = qn(Ba(NO3)2)Assume the moles of Ba(NO₃)₂ dissolved is n; the dissolution is endothermic, so ΔHₛₒₗᵤₜᵢₒₙ is positive.Final Answer: +39.6 kJ/mol
Part D
The calculated magnitude of ΔHₛₒₗᵤₜᵢₒₙ will be smaller than the actual value.
Justification: Spilled Ba(NO₃)₂ means fewer moles dissolve than the weighed amount.
Less heat is absorbed (q measured is smaller), but calculation uses the weighed moles (larger n).
ΔH = qn: smaller q and larger n make the calculated |ΔH| smaller than the true value.
Part E
The magnitude of ΔHₛₒₗᵤₜᵢₒₙ will be equal to the first trial.
Justification: ΔHₛₒₗᵤₜᵢₒₙ is a molar enthalpy change—it depends only on the identity of the solute (Ba(NO₃)₂), not the mass/amount dissolved.
Part F
(i) Balanced decomposition equation
2 Ba(NO₃)₂(s)→Δ2BaO(s)+4NO2(g)+O2(g)
(ii) Mass of O₂ produced from 0.70 mol Ba(NO₃)₂
Mole ratio: 2mol Ba(NO3)2:1mol O2
Moles of O₂ = 0.702=0.35mol
Mass of O₂ = 0.35mol×32.00g/mol=11.2g
(iii) Sign of ΔS° and justification
ΔS° is positive (+).
Justification: A solid reactant decomposes into gaseous products. The number of particles and disorder (entropy) of the system increase greatly.

Question 116 (C₂H₃Cl & C₂Cl₄)
Part A
C₂H₃Cl has a larger dipole moment:
C₂Cl₄ is symmetric; bond dipoles cancel out (net dipole = 0).
C₂H₃Cl is asymmetric; C-Cl and C-H bond dipoles do not cancel, creating a net molecular dipole.
Part B
Average speed of C₂H₃Cl > C₂Cl₄.
Average molecular speed is inversely proportional to molar mass at constant T.
Molar mass of C₂H₃Cl < C₂Cl₄ → faster speed.
Part C
(i) Pressure of C₂Cl₄ (ideal gas law)
PV=nRT → P=nRTVn=0.600 mol, V=1.50 L, T=375+273=648 K, R=0.0821 L·atm/mol·KP=0.600×0.0821×6481.50≈21.3atm
(ii) Measured pressure < ideal pressure
C₂Cl₄ has strong intermolecular forces (London dispersion forces, large molar mass). Real gas molecules attract each other, reducing the force exerted on the container walls.
